claims.text: The native iron oxide film on pre-exposure Q235 steel acts as a protective barrier at room temperature.
The native iron oxide film becomes unstable at approximately 60°C.
Elevated-temperature instability of the oxide film accelerates localized corrosion in chloride-containing environments.
As-received Q235 steel has a naturally formed, thin iron oxide layer.
As-received Q235 steel has inherent microstructural heterogeneity.
Grain boundaries and inclusions can serve as corrosion-initiation sites in Q235 steel.
At room temperature, a stable and adherent passive oxide layer limits chloride-ion attack.
Elevated temperature increases ion mobility and thermal energy in the corrosion system.
Increased ion mobility and thermal energy destabilize the passive film through dissolution or cracking.
Destabilization of the passive film exposes the underlying metal and leads to localized corrosion such as pitting.
Q235 specimens exposed to 3.5 wt.% NaCl at approximately 25°C will have a lower corrosion rate than specimens exposed at approximately 60°C.
Room-temperature specimens will retain more stable passive-film characteristics.
Room-temperature specimens will have fewer pitting sites than elevated-temperature specimens.
Specimens exposed at approximately 60°C will show measurable degradation of the oxide layer.
Specimens exposed at approximately 60°C will show increased pitting density.
Specimens exposed at approximately 60°C will have higher corrosion current densities.
Alteration of the initial oxide layer by pretreatment may change the results.
Non-standard impurity levels may change the corrosion response.
The proposed mechanism is limited to chloride-rich aqueous environments and may not apply to other corrosive media.
